summary.text: Plant physiology is the part of botany that studies how plants function, from photosynthesis and respiration to hormones and transpiration.
Its areas include plant chemistry, single cells, interactions among cells, tissues and organs, internal regulation, and response to the environment.
Plant compounds matter to people too, since aspirin is made from salicylic acid and drug companies research plant chemicals for medicines.

facts.label: The specialist
facts.value: A professional in this field is a plant physiologist

facts.label: Cell differences
facts.value: Plant cells have a cell wall and chlorophyll

facts.label: Macronutrients
facts.value: Needed in large quantities, such as carbon and nitrogen

facts.label: Chemical signals
facts.value: Hormones made in one part signal cells in another

items.prompt: Roots take minerals from the soil, but leaves high above need them too. What lets the plant move them there?

options.label: Chlorophyll in the stem carries them upward
Each leaf makes its own, so nothing needs to move
Light stored in the roots pushes them up
Vascular tissue carries them between roots and leaves

items.explain: Minerals from the roots must reach the leaves and nutrients made in the leaves must reach the roots, and plants move them through vascular tissue.

items.prompt: A gardener sees fruit ripen and leaves drop in winter. What helps control both?

options.label: The gas ethylene that the plant produces
Light-sensitive compounds that track night length
The cell wall losing its shape
Trace minerals absorbed through the roots

items.explain: The ripening of fruit and the loss of leaves in winter are controlled in part by the gas ethylene. Night length controls blooming.

items.prompt: Many flowers bloom at just the right time of year. What do they respond to?

options.label: The gas ethylene made by their fruit
The amount of carbon found in the soil
Night length, sensed by light-sensitive compounds
The thickness of their own cell walls

items.explain: Many flowering plants bloom at the appropriate time because light-sensitive compounds respond to the length of the night, called photoperiodism.

items.prompt: A houseplant needs no meals, but a pet cat does. Which feature of plant cells explains the difference?

options.label: A cell wall, which makes nutrients from soil
Chlorophyll, which reacts with light to make nutrients
Hormones, which stand in for food
Vascular tubes, which pull in prey

items.explain: Plant cells contain chlorophyll, which interacts with light so plants manufacture their own nutrients rather than consuming other living things.

items.prompt: A deer is grazing on a plant that cannot run away. How can the plant defend itself?

options.label: By making toxins and foul-tasting or smelling chemicals
By pulling its roots out of the ground
By absorbing more macronutrients
By growing a thicker cell wall around each leaf

items.explain: Because plants cannot move, they defend themselves chemically against herbivores by producing toxins and foul-tasting or smelling chemicals.

items.prompt: A fertilizer label lists 'macro' and 'micro' nutrients. What does the prefix describe?

options.label: The size of the nutrient particles
Whether the nutrient comes from air or soil
How much of the nutrient the plant needs
Whether leaves or roots absorb the nutrient

items.explain: The prefix macro- refers to the quantity needed, not the size of the nutrient particles; micronutrients are needed only in trace amounts.
